concept.name: Randomized Algorithms

relationships.description: Connects Randomized Algorithms to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Randomized algorithms trade deterministic worst-case guarantees for dramatic gains in simplicity, memory efficiency, and average-case speed by injecting controlled pseudo-randomness into branching, sampling, or hashing.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use Las Vegas algorithms when you need 100% exact answers with probabilistic runtime (e.g., randomized QuickSort), and Monte Carlo algorithms when tiny, bounded error probabilities unlock massive memory or latency savings (e.g., HyperLogLog, Miller-Rabin).

concept.whyItMatters: Adversarial or skewed inputs routinely degrade deterministic algorithms to quadratic time or force prohibitive memory footprints. A single random pivot defeats sorted-input QuickSort attacks, Power-of-Two-Choices load balancing slashes max server queue depth from O(ln n / ln ln n) to O(ln ln n / ln 2), and HyperLogLog counts 1 billion distinct users in 1.5 KB instead of 32 GB.
whenToUse: Defeating worst-case input patterns in sorting, hashing, and routing without complex deterministic balancing (e.g., randomized QuickSort, universal hashing).
Approximating cardinalities, quantiles, or frequencies over high-throughput streams where exact state exceeds RAM (e.g., HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch, reservoir sampling).
Breaking symmetry and thundering-herd synchronization in distributed protocols (e.g., exponential backoff with full jitter, Raft randomized election timeouts of 150-300 ms).
whenNotToUse: Financial ledgers, billing, or compliance counters where even a 0.81% relative error or rare false positive is legally unacceptable.
Safety-critical real-time control loops (avionics, braking) requiring strict deterministic worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds.
Small datasets (under 100,000 items) where exact hash sets or deterministic sorts fit comfortably in L3 cache or a few megabytes of RAM.
keyPoints: Las Vegas algorithms (e.g., randomized QuickSort, randomized Skip Lists) always return the exact right answer; only their runtime is a random variable.
Monte Carlo algorithms (e.g., Miller-Rabin primality, Bloom filters, HyperLogLog) run in fixed time/space and bound error probability exponentially via independent trials or hash bits.
Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) sampling probes two random backends and picks the less loaded one, cutting max load from O(ln n / ln ln n) to O(ln ln n / ln 2) with O(1) coordination.
Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R) maintains a uniform k-item sample over an unbounded stream of unknown length N in O(k) memory.
PRNG choice matters: use SplitMix64 or Xoshiro256++ for simulation/sketches, SipHash-2-4 for hash-flooding resistance, and CSPRNGs (getrandom / SecureRandom) for security or election tie-breaking.

examples.title: Distinct Daily Active Users at Edge Scale with HyperLogLog
examples.scenario: An analytics ingestion tier processes 400,000 events/sec across 50M daily unique user IDs. Storing exact 64-bit IDs per metric bucket in Redis Sets would consume ~3.2 GB per day per dimension.
examples.outcome: Switching to Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT (16,384 6-bit registers = 12 KB per key) reduces memory by >99.9% while keeping standard error at 1.04 / sqrt(16384) = 0.81%.

examples.title: Envoy Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) Load Balancing
examples.scenario: A 200-pod microservice fleet behind an L7 proxy experiences tail-latency spikes under pure round-robin when 10% of pods hit GC pauses or noisy-neighbor CPU throttling.
examples.outcome: Enabling Envoy's LEAST_REQUEST policy with choice_count=2 samples two random healthy endpoints and picks the one with fewer active requests, cutting p99 latency by 45% without global state.

tradeOffs.pro: Doubling HyperLogLog registers or Count-Min Sketch width cuts error smoothly while staying orders of magnitude smaller than exact sets.
tradeOffs.con: Zero-error exactness is impossible in sublinear space; cardinality deltas smaller than ~1% cannot be reliably distinguished.

tradeOffs.pro: Randomization eliminates complex deterministic rebalancing trees or global coordination locks.
tradeOffs.con: Non-deterministic execution complicates unit tests, bug reproduction, and incident postmortems unless PRNG seeds are logged.

tradeOffs.pro: Fast non-cryptographic PRNGs (Xoshiro256++, MurmurHash3) run in ~1-3 ns per call.
tradeOffs.con: Predictable seeds or weak hashes expose hash tables and load balancers to algorithmic complexity DoS attacks.

failureModes.name: Seed Synchronization / Correlated Jitter
failureModes.description: Containers booted from the same image at the same second initialize PRNGs with identical timestamps or static seeds, causing synchronized retry storms.
failureModes.mitigation: Seed PRNGs from OS entropy (/dev/urandom, getrandom()) combined with instance PID/UUID, and verify jitter spread in chaos tests.

failureModes.name: Hash-Flooding Collision Attack
failureModes.description: An attacker crafts keys that collide in a non-keyed hash function (e.g., plain MurmurHash), degrading a randomized hash map or sketch to worst-case behavior.
failureModes.mitigation: Use keyed cryptographic or DoS-resistant hashes like SipHash-2-4 with a per-process secret seed rotated on restart.

failureModes.name: Biased Sampling via Modulo Reduction
failureModes.description: Mapping a 32-bit PRNG output to [0, N) using `rand() % N` introduces modulo bias when 2^32 is not divisible by N, skewing reservoir or shuffle distributions.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Lemire's fast range reduction or rejection sampling (`ThreadLocalRandom.nextInt(n)` / `crypto/rand.Int`) to guarantee strict uniformity.

failureModes.name: Under-Dimensioned Monte Carlo Trials
failureModes.description: Running too few independent rounds (e.g., k=3 in Miller-Rabin or narrow Count-Min width w) allows false positives to slip into production.
failureModes.mitigation: Size parameters from target error bounds (e.g., k=40 for Miller-Rabin gives <= 4^-40 error; w = ceil(e / epsilon) for Count-Min Sketch).

commonMistakes: Using `Math.random()` or `java.util.Random` (48-bit LCG with global atomic CAS contention) in hot multi-threaded paths instead of `ThreadLocalRandom` or Xoshiro256++.
Forgetting to persist or log the PRNG seed in randomized tests and simulations, making flaky failures impossible to reproduce.
Using a non-cryptographic PRNG for security tokens, session IDs, or leader-election tie-breakers where predictability is exploitable.
Assuming HyperLogLog or Bloom filters support item deletion without switching to Counting Bloom Filters or exact backing stores.
Applying naive `rand()` inside Fisher-Yates shuffles with a 32-bit seed for decks > 13 elements (13! > 2^32), making most permutations unreachable.

sections.content:
## The idea

Deterministic algorithms must handle every conceivable input, so adversaries or pathological production data can force worst-case behavior. Randomized algorithms shift the source of uncertainty from the *input* to *internal coin flips*. By choosing pivots, hash seeds, or sample candidates randomly, no fixed input can reliably trigger worst-case paths.

Two foundational families govern the design space:
- **Las Vegas algorithms** never lie: they always produce the exact correct output, while their execution time is a random variable concentrated tightly around the expectation (e.g., randomized QuickSort runs in $O(n \log n)$ with probability $1 - O(n^{-c})$).
- **Monte Carlo algorithms** run within a strict time or memory budget and accept a mathematically bounded probability of error (e.g., Miller-Rabin primality testing, HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch). Repeating $k$ independent trials drives one-sided error down exponentially ($p^k$).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider routing 100,000 RPS across $n = 100$ backend pods using **Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C)** instead of pure random or global least-connections:

1. **Request arrival**: A client request hits the edge proxy (e.g., Envoy).
2. **Two-sample probe**: The proxy draws two distinct indices $i, j \in [0, 99]$ uniformly using a thread-local PRNG (`Xoshiro256++`).
3. **Local queue comparison**: It reads its in-memory active-request counters `inflight[i]` and `inflight[j]` (zero cross-proxy RPCs).
4. **Dispatch & increment**: If `inflight[i] <= inflight[j]`, it increments `inflight[i]` and forwards the request to pod $i$; otherwise pod $j$.
5. **Completion**: On response or timeout, the proxy decrements the chosen pod's counter.

Under pure random placement of $n$ balls into $n$ bins, the fullest bin reaches $\approx \frac{\ln n}{\ln \ln n}$ ($\approx 3$–$4\times$ average). Checking just **two** random choices drops the maximum load exponentially to $\frac{\ln \ln n}{\ln 2} + O(1)$—typically within 1–2 requests of the global optimum—while avoiding the lock contention and stale-state herding of global least-loaded routing.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Las Vegas vs. Monte Carlo & PRNG selection
sections.content:
## Las Vegas vs. Monte Carlo & PRNG selection

Choosing the right class of randomness and generator prevents subtle production bugs:

- **Amplifying Monte Carlo confidence**: A single Miller-Rabin witness catches a composite number with probability $\ge 3/4$. Running $k = 40$ independent bases lowers the false-prime probability to $\le 4^{-40} \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-25}$—lower than hardware cosmic-ray bit flips.
- **Streaming sketches**: **HyperLogLog** hashes each item into a 64-bit integer, uses the first $b$ bits (e.g., $b=14 \implies m=16,384$ buckets) to pick a register, and records the longest run of leading zeros in the remaining bits. **Count-Min Sketch** uses $d$ pairwise-independent hash functions across $w$ counters, taking the `min` across rows to eliminate overcounting bias from collisions.
- **PRNG hygiene**: Never share a single `java.util.Random` across threads (atomic CAS contention stalls cores). Use `ThreadLocalRandom` or `Xoshiro256++` for speed, and `SecureRandom` / `crypto/rand` whenever an attacker could observe outputs and predict future choices.

## Canonical randomized algorithms compared

| Algorithm | Class | Time / Space | Error / Guarantee | Primary Production Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Randomized QuickSort | Las Vegas | $O(n \log n)$ expected, $O(\log n)$ stack | 100% exact output | In-memory sorting immune to pre-sorted inputs |
| Miller-Rabin ($k=40$) | Monte Carlo | $O(k \log^3 n)$ time | $\le 4^{-40}$ false-prime rate | RSA/ECC key generation in OpenSSL / BoringSSL |
| HyperLogLog ($b=14$) | Monte Carlo | $O(1)$ update, 12 KB RAM | $\pm 0.81\%$ standard error | Redis `PFCOUNT`, BigQuery `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` |
| Count-Min Sketch | Monte Carlo | $O(d)$ update, $O(w \cdot d)$ RAM | Overestimates by $\le \varepsilon N$ w.p. $1-\delta$ | Heavy-hitter / DDoS IP tracking in network telemetry |
| Power-of-Two-Choices | Randomized routing | $O(1)$ per request | Max load $O(\ln \ln n / \ln 2)$ | Envoy `LEAST_REQUEST`, NGINX, linkerd2-proxy |

## Failure modes

- **Correlated PRNG seeds**: Containers starting in lockstep with `time(NULL)` seeds generate identical backoff jitter, turning randomized retries into a synchronized thundering herd.
- **Modulo bias**: Computing `rand() % N` when $2^{32} \bmod N \neq 0$ over-weights lower indices; in weighted routing or reservoir sampling, this skews traffic distribution.
- **Hash-collision DoS**: Using unseeded MurmurHash or FNV-1a in public-facing sketches or hash tables lets attackers craft colliding keys that blind heavy-hitter detectors.
- **Non-reproducible test flakiness**: Unseeded randomized property tests fail once every 500 CI runs and cannot be debugged unless the failing seed is printed in test output.

## Production patterns & observability

- **Deterministic replay via logged seeds**: Pass an explicit `uint64_t seed` into simulation, shuffling, and sampling engines; emit the seed in structured logs on any assertion failure.
- **Bounded jitter formulas**: Use AWS-style **Full Jitter** (`random_between(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`) or **Decorrelated Jitter** (`min(cap, random_between(base, sleep * 3))`) rather than fixed-window retries.
- **Sketch mergeability**: HyperLogLog registers and Count-Min arrays with identical seeds and dimensions merge losslessly via element-wise `max` (HLL) or `+` (CMS), enabling lock-free per-core aggregation before periodic reduction.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Classify the requirement: exactness required (Las Vegas) vs. bounded approximation acceptable (Monte Carlo).
- [ ] Verify thread-local PRNGs (`ThreadLocalRandom`, `Xoshiro256++`) are used on hot paths—no global mutexes or atomic seed CAS.
- [ ] Seed from OS CSPRNG (`/dev/urandom` / `getrandom`) at startup; use `SipHash-2-4` if keys are attacker-controlled.
- [ ] Eliminate modulo bias using rejection sampling or Lemire's fast range mapping.
- [ ] Document and monitor error budgets (e.g., HLL register precision $b$, CMS $\varepsilon/\delta$) and log seeds in randomized test suites.

interviewProblems.title: Randomized Algorithms
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Randomized Algorithms. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Randomized algorithms trade deterministic worst-case guarantees for dramatic gains in simplicity, memory efficiency, and average-case speed by injecting controlled pseudo-randomness into branching, sampling, or hashing.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Backend Pod A applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Backend Pod B.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Backend Pod B experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Seed PRNGs from OS entropy (/dev/urandom, getrandom()) combined with instance PID/UUID, and verify jitter spread in chaos tests.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use Las Vegas algorithms when you need 100% exact answers with probabilistic runtime (e.g., randomized QuickSort), and Monte Carlo algorithms when tiny, bounded error probabilities unlock massive memory or latency savings (e.g., HyperLogLog, Miller-Rabin).
Avoid trap: Using `Math.random()` or `java.util.Random` (48-bit LCG with global atomic CAS contention) in hot multi-threaded paths instead of `ThreadLocalRandom` or Xoshiro256++.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to persist or log the PRNG seed in randomized tests and simulations, making flaky failures impossible to reproduce.
When to reach for it: Defeating worst-case input patterns in sorting, hashing, and routing without complex deterministic balancing (e.g., randomized QuickSort, universal hashing).
When to reach for it: Approximating cardinalities, quantiles, or frequencies over high-throughput streams where exact state exceeds RAM (e.g., HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch, reservoir sampling).

putItTogether.title: Putting Randomized Algorithms Intro Together
putItTogether.summary: Use Las Vegas algorithms when you need 100% exact answers with probabilistic runtime (e.g., randomized QuickSort), and Monte Carlo algorithms when tiny, bounded error probabilities unlock massive memory or latency savings (e.g., HyperLogLog, Miller-Rabin).
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Randomized Algorithms Intro before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Switching to Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT (16,384 6-bit registers = 12 KB per key) reduces memory by >99.9% while keeping standard error at 1.04 / sqrt(16384) = 0.81%.
